title: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters: A Causal Intervention for Routing Collapse in Time Series Foundation Models
claim: A standard single-head adapter ignores per-window variation, and the usual mixture-of-experts fix collapses onto one expert when the backbone normalizes its inputs.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, faded unused experts with orange collapse path
description: Two stacked horizontal pipelines separated by a dashed line, each with a bold title. In both panels, three small time-series windows (a blue trend, a red oscillation, and a green square wave) feed a pale-blue box labeled 'Frozen TSFM Backbone (MOMENT, Moirai)'. A 'FROZEN' tag sits on the box and an 'Instance Normalization (RevIN)' sub-box sits under it. Outputs H1–H3 then flow onward. Panel (a) merges them into a single peach 'Single static adapter head' that outputs ŷ. Panel (b) sends them to a peach 'Router' that fans out to experts E1–E5. An orange highlighted arrow goes only to E1, which produces ŷ. E2–E5 are greyed out with dashed arrows and labeled 'unused'. The eye goes first to the orange collapse path in (b).
caption: Problem overview. (a) TSFM adapters use the same head for every window. (b) The standard mixture-of-experts extension fails on instance-normalized TSFMs under unfreezing: entropy collapses ($0.000{\pm}0.000$) and the remaining experts receive no gradient. Same backbone, different heads.
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) commonly adapt to new data by attaching a single trainable head to a frozen backbone, a one-size-fits-all setup that underfits heterogeneous regimes. Replacing the head with a mixture of experts is the standard upgrade, but on instance-normalized backbones (the dominant TSFM design class) it fails: routing entropy collapses to zero and one expert absorbs every input, a failure we call normalization-induced routing collapse. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms do not repair it, because the cause is in the router's input, not its optimization. Pre-encoder normalization strips the statistics a router would need to tell regimes apart. A mutual-information decomposition makes this precise and yields a signal-ratio that, computed before training, predicts dataset vulnerability (Spearman $Ï= -0.88$). Eight causal controls, including a vision-modality replication, isolate instance normalization as the cause. The prescription is a minimal causal intervention: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA), which routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. Under a strictly frozen backbone, RR-MoA wins 54/54 comparisons against the strongest fixed adapter and significantly outperforms LoRA, TRACE, AdaMix, and full fine-tuning. The effect generalizes across six backbones and an imputation task. Frozen RR-MoA also beats full fine-tuning by 12-79% (the Frozen Paradox); two architecturally distinct variants confirm the principle generalizes beyond this specific router.
